note.headline: Tesla flat at 384.68 as a SpaceX merger is reported; still avoid
note.happening: Tesla closed at 384.68, down 0.2%. That holds most of yesterday's jump and sits inside the 380.15–389.95 zone, just under resistance at 393.63–404.4. The Financial Times reported that directors are negotiating a SpaceX-Tesla merger, called the biggest ever. No filing confirms it. The next earnings report is on 2027-01-27.
note.business: The merger report is about governance and sentiment, not about how many cars Tesla sells or what it earns on each one. Until terms are filed, it changes nothing in the reported numbers. SpaceX is a private rocket and satellite company with the same CEO (general knowledge), so a deal would raise questions about who gets what price and whether outside shareholders are treated fairly (general knowledge). The business picture itself is weak. Sales in the latest quarter fell 0.17% from a year earlier, after growing 15.78% two quarters ago. Operating margin slipped to 3.35% from 4.74%. Trailing free cash flow fell to 3.3B from 6.8B. Inventory rose 15% while sales were flat, and unsold cars can lead to price cuts. Each dollar invested now earns 5¢ a year, down from 33¢ three years ago. The balance sheet is not at risk: 37.5B of net cash and 45.4B of liquidity mean the company can fund itself. What is at risk is profit: margins and cash generation are going the wrong way.
note.worth: At 384.68, Tesla is worth about 1521.0B. That is 423.3 times trailing earnings and 14.7 times sales. Its price-to-sales ratio is higher than 77.0% of its own last five years. A cash-flow model (DCF) built on the 3.3B of free cash flow gives 20.01 to 44.3 per share, with a base of 24.66. Even if sales started growing 30% a year, that model gives only 45.31. Comparing the price with Tesla's own price-to-sales history gives 203.8 at the low end, 293.94 in the middle and 399.81 at the top. The gap between the two methods comes from one assumption: whether you value Tesla on the cash it makes today or on the high multiple the market has paid for its future before. The filings note that the price needs about 50% a year growth, while Tesla has delivered 3% a year over three years. I use the own-history range, because the DCF ignores what the market has actually paid for this stock. Even so, the price is above the middle of that range.

note.headline: NVIDIA drops 5.86% to 155.38 as Huang comeback rally fades; still hold
note.happening: NVIDIA fell 5.86% to 155.38, giving back part of the rally that followed Jensen Huang's reported return as CEO. Headlines today are mostly about governance: the government's role in his return, open investigations, and a reported addition of Megaspeed to the U.S. trade blacklist over export controls. Our data has no earnings date, and the latest filed quarter ended 2026-07-26.
note.business: The business numbers are strong. Over the last twelve months revenue was 303.0B, up from 165.2B. Free cash flow (cash left after running and investing in the business) was 127.0B, up from 72.0B. Operating margin rose to 65.21% from 58.09%, and the company holds 23.2B more cash than debt. None of today's CEO news changes these figures. The leadership drama, the investigations and Huang reportedly saying he still does not believe in succession planning affect sentiment and governance, not demand. Two items could touch the business. First, the Megaspeed blacklisting (reported) concerns export controls, which can limit where chips are sold (general knowledge). Second, Amazon's reported Decart deal is a bet on narrowing the chip gap with NVIDIA, a long-run competition risk. The real risks come from the filings. The 65% margin sits at the top of its 5-year range of 16–65%, and peaks like that usually fade. Money customers still owe is up 127% while quarterly sales are up 106%, which can mean sales were pulled forward or customers are stretched. Demand itself does not look at risk today. What is at risk is how long the margin and the payment timing hold.
note.worth: The two methods disagree mainly because they make different assumptions about growth. A discounted cash flow model values the company from its expected future cash. Using the 127.0B in trailing free cash flow and a discount rate near 10%, it gives 191.49 (bear), 222.58 (base) and 264.22 (bull). The company's own price-to-sales history gives 217.35 to 411.04. The more useful reading runs the other way. At 155.38, the price matches the model value of 155.64, which is what 20% starting growth produces, and the data puts the implied starting growth at 20.0%. So the market is not paying for the 83% sales growth of last year. It is paying for growth to slow sharply. The biggest swing factor is margin. If operating margin falls to 48%, the value drops to 116.97, and at 32% it drops to 78.3. The data's valuation summary quotes an older price of 165.05, so today's price sits even lower against those ranges. Multiples tell the same story: 19.6 times trailing earnings, 9.4 times next year's expected earnings, and 12.4 times sales against a peer median of 14.9.
